skos:definition: Controlled vocabulary of analytical parameters referenced by ADA TAPP definitions and analysis-specific detail blocks: protocol/session parameters (schema:PropertyValue and schema:PropertyValueSpecification) and per-analyte column definitions. Each concept @id is the parameter's schema:propertyID URI.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Order of analysis on spectormeter.
Method used to estimate and subtract background X-ray intensity beneath the peak.
Positions of background measurements relative to the peak, in mm and/or sinθ, and whether on the high or low energy side.
Total time spent counting at background position(s) in seconds.
Method and reference materials used to determine and apply blank corrections.
Method used to compute detection limits.
Percent dead time reported by the EDS spectrometer
How elemental concentrations were calculated — directly from measured X-ray intensities or via cation stoichiometry.
Whether this element was measured by WDS or EDS.
Flag indicating whether a spectral interference correction was applied for this element.
Reference material used to quantify and calibrate the interference correction.
List of elements whose X-ray lines overlap with the measured line for this element.
Analysing crystal (monochromator) used in the WDS spectrometer for this element.
Post-acquisition normalization applied using secondary reference materials.
Time spent counting X-ray intensity at the peak position in seconds.
Primary reference material used for element standardization (calibration).
Pulse height analyzer setting used for the WDS detector.
List of quality-control reference materials (secondary standards) routinely analyzed alongside unknowns.
WDS spectrometer number used for this element.
Type of time-dependent intensity correction applied for volatile or beam-sensitive elements.
Offset between measured and accepted reference values for secondary standards, expressed as % relative bias.
Reproducibility of repeated measurements on the same or equivalent standard, expressed as 1σ relative standard deviation (%).
1σ uncertainty propagated from counting statistics on peak and background intensities.
Method detection limit at 99% confidence (3σ) for each measured element.
Type of detector used in the WDS spectrometer for this element.
The X-ray emission line measured for this element.

Offset between measured and accepted reference values for secondary reference materials, expressed as % relative bias. Report both the assessment method and the accuracy values. Specify: (1) secondary RM used and source of reference values, (2) number of analyses, and (3) elements or element groups assessed. Report any systematic biases and likely causes.

Offset between measured and accepted reference values for secondary reference materials, expressed as % relative bias. Report both the assessment method and the accuracy values. Specify: (1) secondary RM used and source of reference values, (2) number of analyses, and (3) elements or element groups assessed. Report any systematic biases and likely causes.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Between-Session (Long-Term) Analytical Precision and Assessment Method
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Reproducibility of measurements across multiple analytical sessions over weeks to months (long-term or intermediate precision). Report both the assessment method and the precision values. Specify: reference material used, number of sessions n, time span covered, and statistic reported. Long-term precision is typically assessed from a compiled record of secondary reference material values across all sessions.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Between-Session (Long-Term) Analytical Precision and Assessment Method
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Reproducibility of measurements across multiple analytical sessions over weeks to months (long-term or intermediate precision). Report both the assessment method and the precision values. Specify: reference material used, number of sessions n, time span covered, and statistic reported. Long-term precision is typically assessed from a compiled record of secondary reference material values across all sessions.

Session detection limit for each measured isotope, expressed in µg g⁻¹, ng g⁻¹, or wt% as appropriate. Report the value(s) and units per isotope or element group. Mandatory at analysis level to demonstrate the reliability of reported near-detection-limit concentrations. The calculation method is captured separately in Detection Limit Method.

Reference or description of the method used to calculate the limit of quantification (LOQ): the lowest concentration reliably measurable with acceptable precision and accuracy. Mandatory at analysis level when concentrations near the LOD are reported. Concentrations between LOD and LOQ are detectable but not reliably quantifiable.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Within-Session Analytical Precision and Assessment Method
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Reproducibility of repeated measurements within a single analytical session. Report both the assessment method and the precision values. Assessment method must specify: (1) the reference material used, (2) number of replicates n, and (3) the statistic reported (1σ RSD, 2σ RSD, etc.). For mapping: assess from repeated analyses of a reference material area at session start and end, or from replicate analyses of a homogeneous reference phase within the map.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Within-Session Analytical Precision and Assessment Method
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Reproducibility of repeated measurements within a single analytical session. Report both the assessment method and the precision values. Assessment method must specify: (1) the reference material used, (2) number of replicates n, and (3) the statistic reported (1σ RSD, 2σ RSD, etc.). For mapping: assess from repeated analyses of a reference material area at session start and end, or from replicate analyses of a homogeneous reference phase within the map.
Electron beam accelerating voltage in kilovolts (kV). The protocol specifies the standard operating voltage; analysts record and justify any deviations.

Whether elemental concentrations were calculated directly from measured X-ray intensities, or estimated by cation stoichiometry (e.g., oxygen calculated from cation proportions in silicates; carbon from stoichiometry in carbonates).
Offset between measured and accepted reference values for secondary standards, expressed as percent relative bias. Include reference material, reference value source, and per-analyte value.

Reproducibility of repeated measurements on the same or equivalent reference material, expressed as 1-sigma relative standard deviation (%). Include reference material name, number of analyses (n), and value per analyte or element group.

Method used to estimate and subtract background X-ray intensity beneath the peak. For WDS: typically 2-point off-peak linear interpolation or Mean Atomic Number (MAN) background model. For EDS: spectral background fitting or top-hat filter applied during spectral processing.
Total time spent counting at off-peak background position(s) in seconds, summed across all background positions.
Location(s) of off-peak background measurement(s) relative to the peak, in mm or sin-theta, and whether on the high- or low-energy side.
Location(s) of off-peak background measurement(s) relative to the peak, in mm or sin-theta, and whether on the high- or low-energy side.
Probe current in nanoamperes (nA). Often varies by phase type or analyte; record the protocol-standard value(s).

Measures taken to minimize beam damage, particularly volatilization or migration of Na, K, F, and Cl in hydrous minerals, glasses, feldspars, phosphates, and carbonates. Document approach, beam conditions used, and phases for which it was applied.

Measures taken to minimize beam damage, particularly volatilization or migration of Na, K, F, and Cl in hydrous minerals, glasses, feldspars, phosphates, and carbonates. Document approach, beam conditions used, and phases for which it was applied.
Diameter of the electron beam in micrometers. 0 indicates a fully focused beam. Document defocused diameter when used to minimize beam damage or improve spatial averaging for beam-sensitive phases.
X x Y dimensions of a small beam raster used at a single analysis point to average a coarse-grained or beam-sensitive phase. Different from X-ray mapping mode; not applicable when mapping.
X x Y dimensions of a small beam raster used at a single analysis point to average a coarse-grained or beam-sensitive phase. Different from X-ray mapping mode; not applicable when mapping.
Method and reference material(s) used to determine and subtract blank signal contributions (e.g., carbon coat contribution to C signal, or background contamination for trace elements).
Method and reference material(s) used to determine and subtract blank signal contributions (e.g., carbon coat contribution to C signal, or background contamination for trace elements).
1-sigma uncertainty propagated from counting statistics on peak and background intensities for each analyte per analysis.
DOI of the dataset or publication containing the coupled technique data. If coupling is documented only through a shared sample IGSN (Group 2), this field may be 'None'.
DOI of the registered protocol for the coupled technique.
Method detection limit at 99% confidence (3-sigma) for each analyte, derived from counting statistics on peak and background. Include the method and resulting value per analyte.
Formula or procedure used to calculate detection limits. Reference method publication if applicable. When the protocol does not specify a method, the analyst should complete this field.
Formula or procedure used to calculate detection limits. Reference method publication if applicable. When the protocol does not specify a method, the analyst should complete this field.
Method used to monitor and correct for instrument drift (beam current drift, spectrometer drift) during the analytical session.
Method used to monitor and correct for instrument drift (beam current drift, spectrometer drift) during the analytical session.

Time spent acquiring X-ray signal at each pixel during X-ray mapping, in milliseconds. For WDS: per spectrometer per pixel; may differ by analyte if spectrometers are assigned differently. For EDS: total live-time per spectrum per pixel.
EDS detector type, manufacturer, window type, active area, and detector geometry (take-off angle, position).

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: EDS Live Time per Point or Pixel
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: EDS spectral acquisition live time per analysis point in seconds. Previously referred to as "EDS Acquisition Time" in this TAPP and commonly used under that name in EPMA and SEM-EDS contexts. Renamed to align with TEM-EDS usage, where the per-point vs. per-pixel distinction (point/line mode vs. spectrum image) is explicit. In EPMA, acquisition is always per point.
Method used to process EDS spectra and extract net peak intensities from raw spectral data.

Whether oxygen content was adjusted to account for halogen substitution (F and/or Cl replacing OH) in halogen-bearing phases such as apatite, amphibole, and mica, where oxygen is calculated by stoichiometry.

Whether oxygen content was adjusted to account for halogen substitution (F and/or Cl replacing OH) in halogen-bearing phases such as apatite, amphibole, and mica, where oxygen is calculated by stoichiometry.
Reference material used to quantify and calibrate the interference correction for this analyte.
Element(s) whose X-ray lines overlap with the measured peak for this analyte, requiring a correction.
Post-acquisition normalization applied using secondary reference materials to correct for session-to-session calibration drift.
Post-acquisition normalization applied using secondary reference materials to correct for session-to-session calibration drift.
Time spent counting X-ray intensity at the peak position in seconds. Protocol specifies standard values per analyte; analysts may adjust within protocol-defined bounds.
Name(s) of the primary reference material(s) used for element standardization (intensity calibration).
Type of detector used in the WDS spectrometer for each analyte. Affects sensitivity and count rate linearity.
Persistent identifier (e.g., IGSN) for the sample analyzed.
Description of how samples were prepared for analysis under this protocol (mounting, polishing, coating). Analysts may document session-specific variations from the protocol standard.
Quality-control reference material(s) analyzed alongside unknowns to verify calibration accuracy. Include material name, assessed elements, number of analyses (n), and measured vs. accepted values.

Order in which analytes are acquired in the spectrometer sequence during point analysis. Relevant for minimizing beam damage (volatile elements measured first) and for sequential multi-channel setups. Not applicable to X-ray mapping, where all assigned spectrometers collect simultaneously at each pixel.

Whether the X-ray map was acquired by moving the sample stage (stage scan) or by deflecting the electron beam (beam scan). Stage scan preserves beam geometry and spot size across the full map but is slower; beam scan is faster but may introduce geometric distortion at large deflections.
Distance between adjacent measurement points in the X-ray map in micrometers, defining the spatial resolution. Report both X and Y step if they differ.

Type of time-dependent intensity (TDI) correction applied to compensate for beam-induced volatilization or migration of sensitive elements (e.g., Na, K, F in glasses, feldspars, carbonates). Most commonly applied in point analysis; uncommon for X-ray mapping.

Type of time-dependent intensity (TDI) correction applied to compensate for beam-induced volatilization or migration of sensitive elements (e.g., Na, K, F in glasses, feldspars, carbonates). Most commonly applied in point analysis; uncommon for X-ray mapping.

Pulse height analyzer (PHA) setting for the WDS detector. Integral mode accepts all pulses above a threshold; Differential mode selects a narrow energy window to reject higher-order reflections and escape peaks.
WDS spectrometer number assigned to each analyte. Different spectrometers may have different crystal configurations.
Number, type, and crystal range of WDS spectrometers on the instrument. For SEM-WDS configurations (third-party WDS on a non-EPMA platform), include WDS manufacturer and model.
Type, design origin, and internal volume of the ablation cell. Cell volume is a primary determinant of aerosol washout time and therefore the achievable time resolution of the data.
Total on-sample ablation time per spot, as set in the acquisition method.

Depth of the ablation pit produced under the registered laser conditions, the method used to measure it, and the resulting per-pulse ablation rate. Characterises the achievable depth/time resolution of the procedure.

Depth of the ablation pit produced under the registered laser conditions, the method used to measure it, and the resulting per-pulse ablation rate. Characterises the achievable depth/time resolution of the procedure.
Repeating order of primary calibration standard(s), quality control standard(s), and unknown analyses within a measurement session.
Repeating order of primary calibration standard(s), quality control standard(s), and unknown analyses within a measurement session.
Flow rate of the intermediate (auxiliary) argon gas stream that positions the plasma relative to the load coil. Affects ion extraction efficiency and oxide production rates.
Flow rate of the intermediate (auxiliary) argon gas stream that positions the plasma relative to the load coil. Affects ion extraction efficiency and oxide production rates.

Method and timing for measuring the ion beam baseline (background) during acquisition, distinct from the data-processing-level blank subtraction method (see Gas Blank, Group 5). For LA-ICP-MS, baseline is measured with the laser off (gas blank), typically before each ablation or block.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Between-Session (Long-Term) Analytical Precision and Assessment Method
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Reproducibility of measurements across multiple analytical sessions over weeks to months. Not addressed in Table 3 of Horstwood et al. (2016), which reports only within-session validation results.

How often the primary calibration standard is measured relative to unknown samples within a session, i.e. the bracketing interval used to monitor and correct for instrumental drift. Implied but not stated explicitly in Table 3 (Horstwood et al. 2016) via the validation-material n counts.
Identity and plumbing configuration of the gas used to transport the ablated aerosol from the cell to the torch, including the procedure-registered flow rate(s).

Kinetic energy discrimination offset voltage applied at the exit of the collision cell in KED mode. Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in KED mode.

Kinetic energy discrimination offset voltage applied at the exit of the collision cell in KED mode. Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in KED mode.

Assignment of isotope masses to Faraday cup or ion counter detector positions for this procedure. For static multi-collection, one configuration applies throughout the measurement; for multi-dynamic procedures, lists all configurations and the cycling sequence. Includes interference-monitor masses collected alongside analyte isotopes.

Flow rate of the collision gas in KED mode. Higher flow rates provide greater interference suppression at the cost of analyte sensitivity. Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in KED mode.

Flow rate of the collision gas in KED mode. Higher flow rates provide greater interference suppression at the cost of analyte sensitivity. Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in KED mode.

Type of collision gas used in KED mode for polyatomic interference suppression. Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in KED mode.

Whether a collision or reaction cell is installed and its operating mode. Long-standard on quadrupole-based instruments; a small number of modern multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Instruments Sapphire, Thermo Scientific Neoma MS/MS) also add a hexapole collision/reaction cell upstream of the collector array, operated in the same STD/KED/DRC modes. Single-collector sector-field instruments have no commercially available collision/reaction cell option and resolve interferences by mass resolution alone.

Physical constants and reference values used in data reduction to calculate the final reported quantity (e.g., decay constants for age calculation, the 238U/235U ratio used to convert measured 235U-based data to 207Pb/235U, or other citable reference values), together with their source. Distinct from Reference Material Information (Group 6), which documents accepted values for specific calibration/validation materials rather than universal physical constants. Critical for traceability: community-recommended values for decay constants and isotope ratios are periodically revised (e.g., the 238U/235U ratio revision by Hiess et al. 2012), and a reported age or ratio can only be correctly reinterpreted against a future revision if the constants originally used are known.
Flow rate of the outer (coolant/plasma) argon gas stream that sustains the ICP plasma. Determines plasma volume and stability.
Flow rate of the outer (coolant/plasma) argon gas stream that sustains the ICP plasma. Determines plasma volume and stability.
DOI or persistent identifier for the co-registered dataset or publication reporting both datasets together.
Registered procedure DOI for the coupled technique named above.

Session detection limit for U, Th, and/or Pb, demonstrating the reliability of reported concentrations near the detection limit. Not requested by Table 3 of Horstwood et al. (2016), which focuses on age uncertainty rather than elemental detection limits.
Reference or description of the method used to calculate the session detection limit reported above.

Mathematical algorithm used to simultaneously solve for the true sample isotope ratio and the mass fractionation factor from the measured spike-sample mixture. Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

The pair of enriched isotopes used to construct a double spike for combined mass bias and/or common-Pb correction. Both isotopes must be naturally rare and free from isobaric interferences. Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Target proportion of double-spike signal relative to total analyte signal in the spiked mixture. An optimal mixing ratio minimises error propagation through the double-spike inversion. Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Target proportion of double-spike signal relative to total analyte signal in the spiked mixture. An optimal mixing ratio minimises error propagation through the double-spike inversion. Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.
The mass ratio monitored to estimate doubly-charged ion (M²⁺) formation during instrument tuning.
The mass ratio monitored to estimate doubly-charged ion (M²⁺) formation during instrument tuning.
Measured percentage of doubly-charged ion production for the monitored species at the time of instrument tuning.
Measured percentage of doubly-charged ion production for the monitored species at the time of instrument tuning.

Electric scan range used for peak acquisition, expressed as percentage of the centre mass. Varies the accelerating voltage to cover nearby masses without re-scanning the magnet. Applicable only to sector-field instruments.

Resistance values (Ω) of the feedback resistors in the Faraday cup amplifiers. Standard amplifiers use 10¹¹ Ω resistors; high-gain amplifiers (10¹² or 10¹³ Ω) are fitted to selected cups to improve signal-to-noise for very low-intensity beams (e.g., low-abundance Pb isotopes in young or low-U material).

Description of the multi-collector Faraday cup array: total number of Faraday cup detectors (fixed and moveable), their labelled positions, and the presence and position of any ion counter (SEM) or Daly detector. The number and span of cups constrains which isotope combinations can be simultaneously collected.

Method used to calibrate the relative gain (amplification factor) of each Faraday cup amplifier at the start of or during each analytical session. Relative gain differences between amplifiers cause systematic errors in isotope ratios if uncorrected. For instruments with ion-counting detectors, also describes the SEM-to-Faraday cross-calibration sequence.
Grants and other funding sources that supported instrument purchase, major upgrades, and procedure development. Include grant numbers and funding agencies.
Whether the guard electrode (also called extraction lens or Fassel torch shield) was active during analysis.
Dead time of each ion-counting detector channel, used in dead-time correction of high count rates.
Dead time of each ion-counting detector channel, used in dead-time correction of high count rates.
Description of the approach used to optimise ICP plasma conditions prior to analysis, including the reference material used for tuning and the acceptance criteria.
Description of the approach used to optimise ICP plasma conditions prior to analysis, including the reference material used for tuning and the acceptance criteria.

Pre-ablation characterisation imaging (typically cathodoluminescence [CL] or backscattered electron [BSE]) used to reveal internal zoning, inherited cores, and metamict domains for selecting valid spot locations, including the imaging instrument and settings used.

Pre-ablation characterisation imaging (typically cathodoluminescence [CL] or backscattered electron [BSE]) used to reveal internal zoning, inherited cores, and metamict domains for selecting valid spot locations, including the imaging instrument and settings used.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Instrument Serial Number or Lab Identifier
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Serial number or laboratory-internal identifier for the specific instrument unit. Supports traceability to instrument service records.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Instrument Serial Number or Lab Identifier
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Serial number or laboratory-internal identifier for the specific instrument unit. Supports traceability to instrument service records.
Minimum warm-up time required after plasma ignition before analyses begin, and any maximum session duration enforced to maintain stable operating conditions.
Duration of signal integration per measurement cycle. Total integration time per spot = (Number of Cycles per Block) × (Integration Time per Cycle) × (Number of Blocks per Measurement).
Duration of signal integration per measurement cycle. Total integration time per spot = (Number of Cycles per Block) × (Integration Time per Cycle) × (Number of Blocks per Measurement).

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Integration Time per Peak/Dwell Times; Quadrupole Settling Time Between Mass Jumps
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Count time (dwell time) per mass position for each measured isotope, and the settling time allowed between mass jumps, as reported in Table 3 of Horstwood et al. (2016). Applies to sequential (Q/SF) mass-hopping acquisition; for simultaneous multi-collector acquisition see Number of Blocks per Measurement, Number of Cycles per Block, and Integration Time per Cycle.
Geometry and designation of the sampler and skimmer cones installed during analysis.
Equation or procedure used to correct for isobaric interferences, including the reference material or monitor isotope used to characterise it.
Elemental or molecular species overlapping with the measured isotope, relevant to U-Th-Pb geochronology (e.g., ²⁰⁴Hg on ²⁰⁴Pb, relevant to the Common-Pb Correction field above).

Whether isobaric interference corrections were applied for any measured isotope in this procedure. A procedure-level Boolean; element-specific detail is in Interfering Species and Interference Correction Method.

Mass balance approach used to calculate sample mass fractions from spike-sample isotope ratio measurements, relevant when a concentration spike (e.g., ²³⁵U, as in Table 3's own worked example) is co-aspirated. Record 'None' if isotope dilution is not used.

Spatial energy distribution of the laser beam at the sample surface, and whether a beam homogenizer is installed. A flat-top (top-hat) profile produces more uniform ablation craters than a Gaussian beam. Fixed hardware property.
Laser pulse energy per unit area at the sample surface, the primary control on ablation rate and crater morphology.
Duration of each individual laser pulse. A fixed hardware property of the laser system that determines the thermal vs. non-thermal ablation regime.
Laser pulse repetition rate.
Reference or description of the method used to calculate the limit of quantification: the lowest concentration reliably measurable with acceptable precision and accuracy.
Source and estimated flow rate of any make-up gas added downstream of the ablation cell, including any desolvating nebuliser used for tracer co-aspiration.
Source and estimated flow rate of any make-up gas added downstream of the ablation cell, including any desolvating nebuliser used for tracer co-aspiration.

Mathematical law used to parameterize instrumental isotope mass fractionation as a function of mass difference. Not stated in Table 3 (Horstwood et al. 2016) for the worked example; the exponential law is most widely used and theoretically best justified for MC-ICP-MS.

Mass resolution mode assigned to each analyte in this procedure. The selected resolution determines which polyatomic interferences (e.g., ¹⁸⁶W¹⁶O⁺ on ²⁰²Hg, relevant to common-Pb correction) are physically resolved by the magnetic sector. Applicable only to sector-field instruments.

Operating mass resolution of the mass analyser. Fixed at unit resolution for quadrupole instruments; selectable (low/medium/high) for sector-field instruments to balance sensitivity against interference suppression; not applicable in the same sense for multi-collector instruments running static low-resolution collection (see Faraday Cup Array Configuration and Collector Configuration for MC-specific detail).

Operating mass resolution of the mass analyser. Fixed at unit resolution for quadrupole instruments; selectable (low/medium/high) for sector-field instruments to balance sensitivity against interference suppression; not applicable in the same sense for multi-collector instruments running static low-resolution collection (see Faraday Cup Array Configuration and Collector Configuration for MC-specific detail).
Mass-to-charge positions (isotope masses) this procedure is designed to measure. Defines the scope of the procedure; the analyst may record the specific subset actually measured in a given session.

Whether an empirical correction was applied to account for systematic differences in laser-induced elemental fractionation (LIEF) patterns between the external calibration standard and the sample matrix.
Procedure applied to identify and minimise memory effects from high-concentration elements in the previous sample or standard that may contaminate subsequent analyses.
Procedure applied to identify and minimise memory effects from high-concentration elements in the previous sample or standard that may contaminate subsequent analyses.
Whether the procedure uses a single acquisition pass or multiple sequential runs on the same sample location, each optimised for different analytical objectives.
Any post-acquisition normalization applied to correct for systematic biases identified from secondary reference materials.
Any post-acquisition normalization applied to correct for systematic biases identified from secondary reference materials.

Number of measurement blocks acquired per spot. Each block typically begins with a baseline (on-peak zero) measurement before the analytical cycles. Multiple blocks allow inspection of signal stability and within-measurement drift.

Number of measurement blocks acquired per spot. Each block typically begins with a baseline (on-peak zero) measurement before the analytical cycles. Multiple blocks allow inspection of signal stability and within-measurement drift.
Number of measurement cycles acquired per block. One cycle corresponds to a single set of simultaneous Faraday cup readings integrated for the duration in Integration Time per Cycle.
Number of measurement cycles acquired per block. One cycle corresponds to a single set of simultaneous Faraday cup readings integrated for the duration in Integration Time per Cycle.

Supplementary methodological context not captured by the structured fields above, as reported in Table 3 of Horstwood et al. (2016) — in the source paper's own example, notes on ablation-cell and sample-line configuration for depth-profiling/single-pulse ablation studies, a variant not otherwise in scope for this single-mode (Spot Analysis) TAPP.

Supplementary methodological context not captured by the structured fields above, as reported in Table 3 of Horstwood et al. (2016) — in the source paper's own example, notes on ablation-cell and sample-line configuration for depth-profiling/single-pulse ablation studies, a variant not otherwise in scope for this single-mode (Spot Analysis) TAPP.

Method used to quantify plasma oxide production and the acceptance threshold applied before commencing analysis. ThO⁺/Th⁺ (mass 248/232) is the standard proxy for U-Th-Pb geochronology, directly relevant to Th/U ratio accuracy.
Documents cases where different analytes are calibrated using different strategies within the same session. If a single strategy applies uniformly, record that here.

Whether the ICP plasma is operated under cool plasma or normal (hot) plasma conditions. Normal plasma is standard for U-(Th-)Pb geochronology; cool plasma would reduce sensitivity for these high-mass analytes and is not typically used.

Procedure applied immediately before each analysis to remove surface contamination or condition the sample surface, distinct from general sample preparation. Pre-ablation pulses are typically discarded before signal acquisition begins.

Procedure applied immediately before each analysis to remove surface contamination or condition the sample surface, distinct from general sample preparation. Pre-ablation pulses are typically discarded before signal acquisition begins.
Primary reference material used to calibrate the instrument and convert raw signal intensities to ages/isotope ratios. Include citation for the accepted values used.
DOI or URL for peer-reviewed publications or technical reports describing, validating, or benchmarking this procedure.

Flow rate of the reactive gas introduced into the dynamic reaction cell (DRC). Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in DRC mode.

Flow rate of the reactive gas introduced into the dynamic reaction cell (DRC). Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in DRC mode.

Type of reactive gas introduced into the dynamic reaction cell (DRC) for interference removal through ion-molecule reactions. Applies to quadrupole-based instruments and to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS) operating in DRC mode.

ICP radiofrequency forward power. Session-tunable within procedure-defined bounds during plasma optimisation; consistent with the analogous, tunable treatment of RF Power across LA-Q/SF-ICP-MS and all three solution ICP-MS TAPPs.
Globally unique, persistent identifier for the analysed sample. IGSN is the recommended standard for geological and cosmochemical samples.
Standard cross-TAPP description of how samples were prepared for analysis (mounting, polishing, coating, etc.).
Material composition of the sampler and skimmer cones. Nickel (Ni) is standard for most matrices; platinum (Pt) is used for high-TDS or organic-matrix samples.
Quality-control reference material(s) analysed as unknowns alongside samples in the same session to assess accuracy and monitor drift. Include citation/accepted values for each.
Instrument sensitivity expressed as useful yield — the percentage of sampled atoms of a given element that are ultimately detected as ions — for the analytical session, following the method cited.

Mode used to collect ion signal across the monitored masses. In peak hopping mode, the quadrupole jumps sequentially between pre-set mass positions and dwells at each peak. Applicable only to quadrupole-based instruments; this concept does not extend to collision-cell-equipped multi-collector instruments (e.g., Nu Sapphire, Thermo Neoma MS/MS), whose collector array performs genuinely simultaneous multi-collection regardless of whether a collision/reaction cell is present upstream. Some such instruments (e.g., Neoma MS/MS) instead use a pre-cell mass filter of a fundamentally different, non-quadrupole design to pre-select a mass window before the cell — a distinct concept not currently captured by any field in this TAPP.

Approach used to select the stable signal interval for integration during data reduction, and to exclude anomalous signals from inclusions, cracks, or mixed domains. Central to interpreting excess scatter/MSWD in the resulting age population.
Description of any signal smoothing device or approach installed between the ablation cell and the ICP-MS to reduce pulse-to-pulse signal variability.
Description of any signal smoothing device or approach installed between the ablation cell and the ICP-MS to reduce pulse-to-pulse signal variability.
Method used to identify and remove anomalous signal spikes arising from micronuggets, inclusions, cracks, or instrument artifacts during time-resolved signal processing.
Method used to identify and remove anomalous signal spikes arising from micronuggets, inclusions, cracks, or instrument artifacts during time-resolved signal processing.
Diameter of the laser spot as set in the acquisition method (nominal/target value).

Distance between the load coil and the sampling cone tip (mm), also called injector depth or torch position. Affects ion transmission efficiency, oxide formation, and doubly-charged species production.

Distance between the load coil and the sampling cone tip (mm), also called injector depth or torch position. Affects ion transmission efficiency, oxide formation, and doubly-charged species production.
Type of plasma torch used (e.g., standard quartz, high-matrix, low-flow).

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Total Integration Time per Output Data Point (s)
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Total duty-cycle time for one complete mass-scan sweep (sum of all per-isotope dwell times and settling times), which sets the time resolution of the down-hole signal. Applies to sequential (Q/SF) acquisition.

Whether each mass peak is scanned three times per cycle and the results averaged, to reduce noise from short-term magnetic field instabilities. Applicable only to sector-field instruments with this capability.
Uncertainty level at which ages/ratios are quoted (e.g., 1σ, 2σ) and the method used to propagate component uncertainties (e.g., quadratic addition) into the final reported value.
Uncertainty level at which ages/ratios are quoted (e.g., 1σ, 2σ) and the method used to propagate component uncertainties (e.g., quadratic addition) into the final reported value.

X-ray tube accelerating voltage in kilovolts (kV) registered by the protocol. Determines the maximum X-ray photon energy and controls penetration depth and phase contrast. Higher voltages provide greater penetration for dense or large samples; lower voltages improve contrast between low-density phases. If the voltage was varied across samples within the same protocol or session, report the full range applied (e.g., 90–115 kV). Note: some sources report this parameter as 'X keV' (maximum Bremsstrahlung photon energy) rather than 'X kV' (tube voltage). For polychromatic lab XCT, these are numerically equivalent: E_max [keV] = V [kV]. Record the value as stated in the source and add a parenthetical note if the unit used is keV.

Assessment of whether residual beam hardening (cupping artifact) is present in the reconstructed volume after any corrections applied during reconstruction. Beam hardening in polychromatic lab XCT produces a characteristic darker interior and brighter edges in the reconstructed CT number profile, even in compositionally uniform material. Record whether this artifact is detectable in the final dataset, what correction or mitigation was applied (e.g., linearisation, pre-filtering, iterative correction), and whether any residual effect influences the analysis region.

Numerical value or setting applied in the software beam hardening correction algorithm for this specific analysis. May be tuned empirically per material type or per scan session. Analysis-level companion to Beam Hardening Correction Method.

Numerical value or setting applied in the software beam hardening correction algorithm for this specific analysis. May be tuned empirically per material type or per scan session. Analysis-level companion to Beam Hardening Correction Method.

DOI or other persistent identifier for the co-registered dataset or publication where both datasets are reported together. Accepts: a dedicated dataset DOI (if separately deposited), a shared dataset DOI (if co-submitted in the same package), or a publication DOI. Use "same submission" if the coupled dataset is included in this data package, or "pending" if not yet assigned. If coupling is documented through a shared sample identifier only, that information is already captured in Sample Persistent Identifier (Group 2).

Registered protocol DOI for the coupled technique named above. Provides a stable, citable link to the companion method independent of whether a dataset has been deposited. If the coupled protocol has not yet been registered, enter the DOI of a publication describing the coupled method, or "pending". Enter "None" if no coupling is planned.

Analysis-level record of what independent validation was performed and its result. Report the validation method(s) used, the quantitative agreement achieved (e.g., relative difference in modal abundance, porosity), and any discrepancies and their likely causes. Where BSE imaging is the validation method, note that BSE provides a 2D section while CT provides a 3D volume.

Protocol-level specification of what independent analytical validation is required to confirm CT segmentation results, phase identification, or quantitative measurements. Cross-validation is relevant where CT grey-values alone cannot uniquely distinguish phases with similar attenuation coefficients. Common approaches include BSE imaging, SEM-EDS or EPMA modal analysis, He pycnometry for bulk porosity, and Raman or SIMS phase mapping. Record the required validation method(s) and the sampling fraction (e.g., every sample, one per session, or a representative subset).

Protocol-level specification of what independent analytical validation is required to confirm CT segmentation results, phase identification, or quantitative measurements. Cross-validation is relevant where CT grey-values alone cannot uniquely distinguish phases with similar attenuation coefficients. Common approaches include BSE imaging, SEM-EDS or EPMA modal analysis, He pycnometry for bulk porosity, and Raman or SIMS phase mapping. Record the required validation method(s) and the sampling fraction (e.g., every sample, one per session, or a representative subset).

Whether the raw CT grayscale values have been calibrated to physically meaningful units using reference materials. Calibrated CT numbers enable cross-instrument and cross-session comparison and support phase identification by comparison to calculated linear attenuation coefficient (LAC) values (e.g., using MuCalc; Hanna & Ketcham 2017). Uncalibrated grayscale values are instrument- and session-specific.

Whether the raw CT grayscale values have been calibrated to physically meaningful units using reference materials. Calibrated CT numbers enable cross-instrument and cross-session comparison and support phase identification by comparison to calculated linear attenuation coefficient (LAC) values (e.g., using MuCalc; Hanna & Ketcham 2017). Uncalibrated grayscale values are instrument- and session-specific.
Number of pixels in the detector array (width × height). Combined with detector pixel size and geometric magnification, determines the field of view.

Detector pixel binning factor applied during acquisition. Binning combines adjacent pixels (e.g., 2×2 combines 4 pixels into one), reducing effective resolution while increasing per-pixel SNR and reducing file size. 1×1 indicates no binning.

Detector pixel binning factor applied during acquisition. Binning combines adjacent pixels (e.g., 2×2 combines 4 pixels into one), reducing effective resolution while increasing per-pixel SNR and reducing file size. 1×1 indicates no binning.

Physical size of a single pixel on the detector in micrometres. This is a fixed hardware property of the detector array, distinct from the reconstructed voxel size (which depends on geometric magnification and binning).

Duration of X-ray exposure for each individual projection image frame, in seconds, as registered by the protocol. Set as a deliberate choice for the target sample type and voxel size: longer exposures increase SNR at the cost of total scan time. May be adjusted within protocol-allowed bounds for samples that are unusually dense or unusually transparent. If the exposure time was varied across samples within the same protocol or session, report the full range applied (e.g., 0.5–2 s).

Whether dark-field (detector read with X-ray source off; electronic noise baseline) and bright-field (source on, no sample; gain calibration) reference images are acquired and applied to normalize detector response before reconstruction. Standard practice in all quantitative lab XCT;.

Number of individual detector frames acquired and averaged to produce each saved projection image, as registered by the protocol. Frame averaging reduces random electronic noise. The effective exposure per projection = exposure time per frame × frames averaged.

Number of individual detector frames acquired and averaged to produce each saved projection image, as registered by the protocol. Frame averaging reduces random electronic noise. The effective exposure per projection = exposure time per frame × frames averaged.

Assessment of whether high-density inclusions (FeNi metal, platinum-group minerals, dense oxides, or other high-Z phases) produce streak or starburst artifacts in the reconstructed volume. Common forms include radial starburst streaks from high-Z inclusions and shadowing (anomalously low CT number) in beam-shadow regions behind dense phases. Record which artifact type(s) are present, their spatial extent, and any exclusion zones or correction steps applied.

Smallest feature reliably detected and quantified in this analysis at the achieved voxel size and SNR. The practical detection limit is determined jointly by voxel size, effective spatial resolution (PSF), and image contrast. Per Withers et al. (2021), a feature must span at least 3 voxels to be positively identified, and at least 10 voxels for reliable shape and volume characterisation. Report the minimum feature size threshold applied in quantitative analysis and the basis for that value (e.g., SNR-limited, PVE-limited, or analyst-defined).

Total number of equally-spaced projection images acquired over the full rotation range. More projections improve reconstruction quality by reducing under-sampling streak artifacts but increase scan time. For Mode B (multi-volume stitching), this is the number per sub-volume.

Optical magnification objective installed between the scintillator and CCD/CMOS detector. Applies only to instruments using optical magnification (e.g., Zeiss Xradia Versa series). For systems using only geometric magnification, report "Not applicable".

Bit depth of the reconstructed 3D volume (number of bits used to encode each voxel's grayscale value). Common values are 8-bit (256 gray levels), 16-bit (65,536 gray levels), or 32-bit floating point. Bit depth affects the dynamic range available for phase segmentation and quantitative attenuation analysis. The protocol may specify a required output bit depth if downstream analysis workflows depend on a consistent grayscale range; the analyst confirms or adjusts at analysis time.

Bit depth of the reconstructed 3D volume (number of bits used to encode each voxel's grayscale value). Common values are 8-bit (256 gray levels), 16-bit (65,536 gray levels), or 32-bit floating point. Bit depth affects the dynamic range available for phase segmentation and quantitative attenuation analysis. The protocol may specify a required output bit depth if downstream analysis workflows depend on a consistent grayscale range; the analyst confirms or adjusts at analysis time.
File format of the reconstructed CT volume as output by the reconstruction software. Bit depth is recorded separately in Output Bit Depth.

Analysis-level record of PVE severity and how it was handled in this specific analysis. Documents the minimum feature size relative to the voxel size, the fraction of the feature population affected, and any PVE correction method applied (e.g., PSF-based deconvolution via Blob3D).

Protocol-level specification of how partial volume effects (PVE) are managed in quantitative analysis. PVE produces intermediate CT numbers at phase boundaries and at the surfaces of small features, because each voxel integrates the attenuation of all material within its volume. PVE correction can be implemented via PSF-based deconvolution tools such as Blob3D. Record the minimum feature size criterion adopted for the protocol (in voxels or µm), the treatment of boundary voxels in modal abundance or size distribution calculations, and whether PVE correction is required or optional.

Protocol-level specification of how partial volume effects (PVE) are managed in quantitative analysis. PVE produces intermediate CT numbers at phase boundaries and at the surfaces of small features, because each voxel integrates the attenuation of all material within its volume. PVE correction can be implemented via PSF-based deconvolution tools such as Blob3D. Record the minimum feature size criterion adopted for the protocol (in voxels or µm), the treatment of boundary voxels in modal abundance or size distribution calculations, and whether PVE correction is required or optional.

Method used to assign reconstructed CT number ranges to specific mineral phases or material types. Approaches include comparison to calculated linear attenuation coefficients (LAC), cross-validation with independent analytical techniques, or empirical calibration.

Method used to assign reconstructed CT number ranges to specific mineral phases or material types. Approaches include comparison to calculated linear attenuation coefficients (LAC), cross-validation with independent analytical techniques, or empirical calibration.

Convolution (apodization) filter kernel applied during back-projection reconstruction. Sharper filters (Ram-Lak) enhance edge definition but amplify high-frequency noise; smoother filters (Hann, Hamming) reduce noise at the cost of edge sharpness. The choice represents a deliberate protocol-level tradeoff.

Convolution (apodization) filter kernel applied during back-projection reconstruction. Sharper filters (Ram-Lak) enhance edge definition but amplify high-frequency noise; smoother filters (Hann, Hamming) reduce noise at the cost of edge sharpness. The choice represents a deliberate protocol-level tradeoff.
Software used to reconstruct 2D projection images into a 3D CT volume, including version number. Often bundled with the instrument and proprietary to the manufacturer.

Protocol specification for how ring artifacts are handled. Ring artifacts appear as concentric circular bands centred on the rotation axis and arise from defective or miscalibrated detector pixels. Method is the protocol-level specification; whether correction was applied and its outcome are recorded at analysis level in Group 6.

Protocol specification for how ring artifacts are handled. Ring artifacts appear as concentric circular bands centred on the rotation axis and arise from defective or miscalibrated detector pixels. Method is the protocol-level specification; whether correction was applied and its outcome are recorded at analysis level in Group 6.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Ring Artifact Severity and Correction Outcome
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Assessment of whether ring artifacts — concentric rings centred on the rotation axis arising from differential sensitivity or gain drift among detector elements — were present and whether correction was effective. Note that ring correction algorithms modify image intensity in narrow annular bands; in samples containing linear geological features oriented tangentially to the rotation axis, ring correction can alter or introduce spurious linear features in those orientations. Record whether rings were present, whether correction was applied, and whether any residual rings or correction artifacts fall within the analysis volume of interest.

Whether projection images are acquired during continuous sample rotation (faster; may introduce slight motion blur at high rotation speeds) or at discrete step positions with the stage stationary during each exposure (stop-and-shoot; eliminates motion blur). Continuous rotation has been associated with sub-volume rotational mismatch artifacts in multi-volume stitching workflows (Eckley et al. 2025).

Total angular range over which projection images are acquired, in degrees. Full 360° rotation is standard for cone-beam lab XCT. 180° rotation (half-scan) is sometimes used for faster acquisition but may introduce additional artifacts.

Angular increment between successive projection images, in degrees. Equal to Rotation Range divided by Number of Projections when both are reported; however, some sources report step size as the primary rotation parameter without stating the total number of projections explicitly. Finer step sizes improve angular sampling and reduce streak artifacts at the cost of longer scan time.

Angular increment between successive projection images, in degrees. Equal to Rotation Range divided by Number of Projections when both are reported; however, some sources report step size as the primary rotation parameter without stating the total number of projections explicitly. Finer step sizes improve angular sampling and reduce streak artifacts at the cost of longer scan time.

Physical dimensions of the sample in mm, reported as length × width × height (or equivalent three orthogonal measurements). The maximum dimension constrains the minimum achievable field of view and therefore the coarsest achievable voxel size. The minimum dimension determines how many voxels span the smallest feature of interest.

Mass of the sample in grams, recorded for curatorial tracking of precious or limited materials. Particularly important for meteorite, mission-returned, and other restricted samples. This is an analysis-level field: the actual sample mass depends on the specific sample being scanned, not on the protocol design.

Method used to mount or hold the sample on the instrument rotation stage. Mounting material should transmit X-rays at the selected voltage without dominating beam attenuation. Report the holder type, adhesive or support material, and any alignment aids used.

Method used to mount or hold the sample on the instrument rotation stage. Mounting material should transmit X-rays at the selected voltage without dominating beam attenuation. Report the holder type, adhesive or support material, and any alignment aids used.
Globally unique, persistent identifier for the analysed sample. IGSN (International Geo Sample Number) is the recommended standard for geological and cosmochemical samples.

Any preparation steps applied to the sample before scanning, including cleaning, trimming, consolidation, or drying. XCT is typically non-destructive with no surface preparation required; note any exceptions.

Any preparation steps applied to the sample before scanning, including cleaning, trimming, consolidation, or drying. XCT is typically non-destructive with no surface preparation required; note any exceptions.
Software used for image segmentation, phase identification, and quantitative 3D analysis after reconstruction. Report all packages used, with version numbers.
General approach used to separate distinct phases or features in the reconstructed CT volume. The method must be reported for any quantitative result to be reproducible.

Specific CT number range(s) or quantitative criteria used to define each segmented phase or feature. Documenting these values enables reproducibility assessment and cross-study comparison. For LAC-calibrated datasets, report values in cm⁻¹.

Specific CT number range(s) or quantitative criteria used to define each segmented phase or feature. Documenting these values enables reproducibility assessment and cross-study comparison. For LAC-calibrated datasets, report values in cm⁻¹.

Quantitative measure of image quality in the reconstructed CT volume. Typically calculated as the mean CT number divided by the standard deviation of CT number in a homogeneous reference region (e.g., an inclusion-free zone of the matrix). SNR is controlled by photon flux (source power, exposure time, number of projections) and sample attenuation. Record the measured value and the region used for measurement, or note if SNR was not formally measured.

Distance from the X-ray source focal spot to the detector surface, in mm, as registered by the protocol. Together with SOD, determines geometric magnification M = SDD/SOD. Voxel size ≈ detector pixel size / M (before binning; divide additionally by optical objective for Versa-class systems).

Distance from the X-ray source focal spot to the detector surface, in mm, as registered by the protocol. Together with SOD, determines geometric magnification M = SDD/SOD. Voxel size ≈ detector pixel size / M (before binning; divide additionally by optical objective for Versa-class systems).

Distance from the X-ray source focal spot to the centre of the sample rotation axis, in mm, as registered by the protocol. Together with SDD, determines geometric magnification (M = SDD/SOD). Shorter SOD increases magnification and reduces voxel size.

Distance from the X-ray source focal spot to the centre of the sample rotation axis, in mm, as registered by the protocol. Together with SDD, determines geometric magnification (M = SDD/SOD). Shorter SOD increases magnification and reduces voxel size.

Effective spatial resolution of the reconstructed CT volume, which typically differs from (and is coarser than) the voxel size due to the detector point spread function (PSF), geometric unsharpness, and the reconstruction filter. The Nyquist limit sets a theoretical floor at 2× the voxel size. Formal measurement uses the PSF method described in Ketcham & Hildebrandt (2014) or the modulation transfer function (MTF); resolution can also be reported per ASTM E1441-11. When formal measurement is unavailable, an estimate based on acquisition geometry (e.g., the Brenner-Weiss formula) or a stated multiple of the voxel size may be recorded. Report the value in µm along with the method used to determine or estimate it.

Method used to register adjacent sub-volume datasets to each other and stitch them into a single continuous 3D volume. Report the alignment strategy (manual, automated, fiducial-based), the software used, and any correction steps applied. Note: rotational mismatch artifacts have been identified in continuous-rotation acquisitions (~0.35° misalignment in Eckley et al. 2025); their correction via raw projection re-alignment should be documented here.

Total elapsed time for the complete XCT acquisition, from the start of the first projection to the end of the last. For multi-volume acquisitions, this is the combined scan time across all sub-volumes (not including setup or reconstruction time). Useful for assessing beam stability and sample integrity concerns over long scans.

X-ray tube current in microamperes (µA) registered by the protocol. Controls photon flux and therefore projection image SNR. Higher current improves SNR but increases thermal loading on the source and may increase focal spot size. If the current was varied across samples within the same protocol or session, report the full range applied (e.g., 65–115 µA).

Protocol-level rules specifying how the Volume of Interest (VOI) is to be defined for quantitative analysis. Common criteria exclude cone-beam artifact zones at sample edges, beam hardening halos near dense inclusions, and sample holder signal. The actual VOI applied in a specific analysis is recorded separately at analysis level.

Protocol-level rules specifying how the Volume of Interest (VOI) is to be defined for quantitative analysis. Common criteria exclude cone-beam artifact zones at sample edges, beam hardening halos near dense inclusions, and sample holder signal. The actual VOI applied in a specific analysis is recorded separately at analysis level.

Isotropic voxel edge length of the reconstructed 3D volume in micrometres. The protocol registers the target voxel size, set based on the minimum feature size to be resolved (target voxel size ≤ ~1/3 of the minimum resolvable feature size). At analysis level, record the achieved voxel size as reported by the reconstruction software, which may differ slightly from the target due to final geometric calibration.

X-ray tube power in watts (W) registered by the protocol. Derivable as voltage (kV) × current (mA) = kV × µA / 1000. Power constrains the achievable focal spot size for microfocal tubes: higher power requires a larger focal spot, trading spatial resolution for SNR. Retained as a standalone field because it is routinely reported in the literature and directly constrains instrument operating limits. If power was varied across samples within the session, report the full range applied (e.g., 7–13 W).

X-ray tube power in watts (W) registered by the protocol. Derivable as voltage (kV) × current (mA) = kV × µA / 1000. Power constrains the achievable focal spot size for microfocal tubes: higher power requires a larger focal spot, trading spatial resolution for SNR. Retained as a standalone field because it is routinely reported in the literature and directly constrains instrument operating limits. If power was varied across samples within the session, report the full range applied (e.g., 7–13 W).

Material and thickness of the beam-hardening filter placed between the X-ray source and the sample. Hardens the beam by attenuating low-energy photons, reducing beam hardening artifacts and improving CT number stability across the sample. Both filter material and thickness must be reported. Instrument-proprietary filter codes should be decoded where possible.

Material of the X-ray tube anode (target). Determines the characteristic line energies superimposed on the bremsstrahlung continuum, which can affect phase contrast at specific energies. Multi-metal anodes (e.g., W/Mo/Cu) extend the usable energy range.

Total on-sample ablation (signal acquisition) time per individual spot in seconds, as set in the acquisition method. This is a protocol-level parameter for spot analysis: it reflects the deliberate trade-off between signal accumulation (longer = lower LOD), sample consumption, and session throughput. For transect analysis, the equivalent protocol-level parameter is scan speed (captured in Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size). For mapping analysis, total acquisition time is sample-area-dependent and therefore analysis-level, not captured here.

Repeating order of primary calibration standard(s), quality control standard(s), and unknown analyses within a measurement session. Editable to allow minor adjustments while maintaining the bracketing strategy defined in the protocol.

Flow rate of the intermediate (auxiliary) argon gas stream that positions the plasma relative to the load coil, in L/min. Affects ion extraction efficiency and oxide production rates. Distinct from the carrier gas (which transports ablation aerosol) and the coolant (plasma) gas.

Total time spent measuring gas blank (background signal with laser off or shutter closed) before each ablation event, in seconds. For spot and transect analysis, a discrete background interval is measured before each ablation. For mapping, background is typically measured once per raster line or at the start of a map session rather than before each individual pixel. Editable to allow session-specific adjustment.

Gas used to transport ablated aerosol from the ablation cell to the ICP-MS torch, with the protocol-registered target flow rate(s). Helium is standard for most UV laser systems due to superior aerosol transport. Flow rates are protocol targets; actual session values may be adjusted within ±10% during tuning.

Bias voltage applied at the collision/reaction cell exit to discriminate between analyte ions and low-energy polyatomic interferences in KED mode, in volts (V). A negative bias preferentially retards slow polyatomic ions while transmitting faster analyte ions. Record 'None' if the CRC is in STD mode.

Flow rate of the collision gas (typically He) introduced into the collision/reaction cell, in mL/min. Controls the degree of ion thermalization and KED efficiency. Record 'None' if the CRC is in STD mode.

Flow rate of the outer (coolant/plasma) argon gas stream that sustains the ICP plasma, in L/min. Determines plasma volume and stability. Set during initial plasma optimisation and confirmed at each session start.

DOI or other persistent identifier for the co-registered dataset or publication where both datasets are reported together. Accepts: a dedicated dataset DOI (if separately deposited), a shared dataset DOI (if co-submitted in the same package), or a publication DOI. Use "same submission" if the coupled dataset is included in this data package, or "pending" if not yet assigned. If coupling is documented through a shared sample identifier only, that information is already captured in Sample Persistent Identifier (Group 2).

Registered protocol DOI for the coupled technique named above. Provides a stable, citable link to the companion method independent of whether a dataset has been deposited. If the coupled protocol has not yet been registered, enter the DOI of a publication describing the coupled method, or "pending". Enter "None" if no coupling is planned.

The mass ratio monitored to estimate doubly-charged ion (M²⁺) formation during instrument tuning. Doubly-charged ions appear at half the mass of the parent ion and can cause isobaric interferences on analytes in that mass region. The monitor species and the mass positions monitored should be stated explicitly. Analogous to Oxide Production Method and Threshold for oxide monitoring.

The mass ratio monitored to estimate doubly-charged ion (M²⁺) formation during instrument tuning. Doubly-charged ions appear at half the mass of the parent ion and can cause isobaric interferences on analytes in that mass region. The monitor species and the mass positions monitored should be stated explicitly. Analogous to Oxide Production Method and Threshold for oxide monitoring.

Measured percentage of doubly-charged ion production for the monitored species at the time of instrument tuning. The protocol should specify the acceptable threshold (e.g., <1%, <3%); the measured value for each session is recorded here. Report both the threshold and the measured value where possible.

Measured percentage of doubly-charged ion production for the monitored species at the time of instrument tuning. The protocol should specify the acceptable threshold (e.g., <1%, <3%); the measured value for each session is recorded here. Report both the threshold and the measured value where possible.

Count time (dwell time) per mass position for each measured isotope in milliseconds. Longer dwell times improve counting statistics and lower detection limits but reduce the number of isotopes measurable within a given scan cycle time. For mapping, scan cycle time directly determines spatial resolution at a given scan speed: shorter cycle time = finer spatial resolution.

Electric scan range used for peak acquisition, expressed as percentage of the centre mass (%). Varies the accelerating voltage to cover masses in the vicinity of the set magnetic mass without re-scanning the magnet. Record 'N/A' if E-scan acquisition mode is not used.
For protocols using fused glass, the flux type and sample:flux dilution ratio used to prepare the analytical glass.
For protocols using fused glass, the flux type and sample:flux dilution ratio used to prepare the analytical glass.

Description of the approach used to optimise ICP plasma conditions prior to analysis, including the reference material used for tuning and the acceptance criteria (e.g., oxide production threshold, sensitivity targets, mass calibration).

Description of the approach used to optimise ICP plasma conditions prior to analysis, including the reference material used for tuning and the acceptance criteria (e.g., oxide production threshold, sensitivity targets, mass calibration).

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Instrument Serial Number or Lab Identifier
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Serial number or laboratory-internal identifier for the specific instrument unit. Supports traceability to instrument service records.

skos:hasTopConcept.skos:prefLabel: Instrument Serial Number or Lab Identifier
skos:hasTopConcept.skos:definition: Serial number or laboratory-internal identifier for the specific instrument unit. Supports traceability to instrument service records.

Minimum warm-up time required after plasma ignition before analyses begin, and any maximum session duration enforced to maintain stable operating conditions. These constraints are part of the protocol and cannot be varied by the analyst.

Spatial energy distribution of the laser beam at the sample surface, and whether a beam homogenizer is installed. A flat-top (top-hat) profile produces more uniform ablation craters and more reproducible crater morphology than a Gaussian beam. This is a fixed hardware property of the laser system.

Laser pulse energy in millijoules as set at the laser output or measured at the sample surface. Less commonly reported than fluence because it does not account for spot area. Report only when the system displays energy directly. Laser fluence (J cm⁻²) is the preferred quantity and is captured in Default Laser Fluence.

Laser pulse energy in millijoules as set at the laser output or measured at the sample surface. Less commonly reported than fluence because it does not account for spot area. Report only when the system displays energy directly. Laser fluence (J cm⁻²) is the preferred quantity and is captured in Default Laser Fluence.

Laser pulse energy per unit area at the sample surface in J cm⁻², as registered by the protocol. Fluence is the physically meaningful quantity controlling ablation rate, crater morphology, elemental fractionation, and particle size distribution. If the system reports only as % of maximum output, include that value and note the system maximum where known.

Duration of each individual laser pulse, including units. Pulse duration determines the ablation regime: nanosecond (ns) pulses involve significant thermal effects and elemental fractionation; femtosecond (fs) pulses are non-thermal and substantially reduce elemental fractionation and matrix effects. This is a fixed hardware property of the laser system.

Laser pulse repetition rate in hertz registered by the protocol. For mapping methods, repetition rate together with scan speed and spot size determines pixel size and spatial resolution. Analysts may adjust within protocol-allowed bounds.

Operating mass resolution of the mass analyser. For quadrupole instruments this is fixed at unit resolution by instrument design. For sector-field instruments the analyst selects low, medium, or high resolution to balance sensitivity against spectral interference suppression.

Whether an empirical correction was applied to account for systematic differences in laser-induced elemental fractionation (LIEF) patterns between the external calibration standard and the sample matrix.

Protocol applied to identify and minimise memory effects from high-concentration elements in the previous sample or standard that may contaminate subsequent analyses, or from incomplete aerosol washout between adjacent pixels in raster mapping mode. For mapping, the mitigation strategy involves controlling scan speed relative to washout time to ensure each pixel signal is sufficiently free of the preceding pixel's contribution.

Protocol applied to identify and minimise memory effects from high-concentration elements in the previous sample or standard that may contaminate subsequent analyses, or from incomplete aerosol washout between adjacent pixels in raster mapping mode. For mapping, the mitigation strategy involves controlling scan speed relative to washout time to ensure each pixel signal is sufficiently free of the preceding pixel's contribution.

Whether the protocol uses a single acquisition pass or multiple sequential runs on the same sample location, each optimized for different analytical objectives. For multi-run designs, describe the number of runs, their purpose, key laser and instrument settings per run, and how outputs of one run feed into data reduction of another. Not applicable to raster mapping, where each spatial location is visited exactly once.
Whether a correction was applied for nonlinear response at the transition between pulse-counting and analog detector modes.
Whether a correction was applied for nonlinear response at the transition between pulse-counting and analog detector modes.

Method used to identify and remove anomalous signal spikes arising from micronuggets, inclusions, cracks, or instrument artifacts during time-resolved signal processing. Editable because the specific implementation may vary between sessions while remaining within the protocol framework.

Method used to identify and remove anomalous signal spikes arising from micronuggets, inclusions, cracks, or instrument artifacts during time-resolved signal processing. Editable because the specific implementation may vary between sessions while remaining within the protocol framework.

Additional gas(es) mixed into the carrier stream downstream of the ablation cell, with the protocol-registered target flow rate. Ar make-up gas is standard. Small N₂ additions can enhance sensitivity for some elements. If N₂ is not added, state "None" explicitly to distinguish from not reported.

Additional gas(es) mixed into the carrier stream downstream of the ablation cell, with the protocol-registered target flow rate. Ar make-up gas is standard. Small N₂ additions can enhance sensitivity for some elements. If N₂ is not added, state "None" explicitly to distinguish from not reported.

Any post-acquisition normalization applied to correct for systematic biases identified from secondary reference materials, or stoichiometric normalization applied per pixel in mapping. Distinct from the primary internal standard approach captured in Internal Standard Approach.

Any post-acquisition normalization applied to correct for systematic biases identified from secondary reference materials, or stoichiometric normalization applied per pixel in mapping. Distinct from the primary internal standard approach captured in Internal Standard Approach.

Protocol applied immediately before each analysis to remove surface contamination or condition the sample surface. Distinct from general sample preparation. For spot analysis, pre-ablation pulses are discarded before signal acquisition begins. For mapping, this step is typically omitted as the large area ablated averages out surface effects.

Protocol applied immediately before each analysis to remove surface contamination or condition the sample surface. Distinct from general sample preparation. For spot analysis, pre-ablation pulses are discarded before signal acquisition begins. For mapping, this step is typically omitted as the large area ablated averages out surface effects.

Primary reference material(s) used to calibrate the instrument and convert raw signal intensities to concentrations or isotope ratios. Include material name, source institution, and citation for the accepted values used. Editable because the specific lot or certification vintage may differ between sessions while the material type remains the same.

Distance between adjacent raster lines in a 2D elemental map, measured perpendicular to the scan direction, in micrometres. Together with spot size, this determines whether adjacent lines are contiguous (line spacing = spot size), overlapping (line spacing < spot size), or have gaps (line spacing > spot size). Applies to raster mapping only.
